The paper is **“Enhancing the detection of barcoded reads in high throughput DNA sequencing data by controlling the false discovery rate.”** *BMC Bioinformatics*. 2014;15:264. PMID: **25099007**. DOI: **10.1186/1471-2105-15-264**.

The study introduces an adapted, tail-area-based false discovery rate (FDR) method to distinguish barcoded from unbarcoded reads in noisy sequencing data, where barcode positions may be uncertain and barcode-like sequences may occur by chance in the reference genome. It uses the FDR to choose an acceptable minimum distance between reads and barcodes. In a proof-of-concept experiment, it detected barcodes in **83% of reads at 89% precision**; including an adjacent primer raised performance to **99% sensitivity at 99% precision**, with further improvement from paired-end analysis. Applying the approach to UV-induced *Atp1a1* variants in murine melanocytes found no evidence of cross-sample DNA contamination. Barcodes in the evaluated sets were designed to correct one insertion, deletion, or substitution.

Yes. A 2014 study introduced a tail-area-based false discovery rate (FDR) method to distinguish barcoded from unbarcoded reads in noisy high-throughput sequencing data. The method uses FDR to select a minimum read-to-barcode distance threshold.

In the proof-of-concept evaluation, it detected barcodes in **83% of reads at 89% precision**. Using adjacent primer evidence raised reported performance to **99% sensitivity and 99% precision**; paired-end analysis further improved results. These findings support the approach in the study’s evaluated setting, though they do not establish that it will improve every barcode-sequencing workflow.

**Reference:** “Enhancing the detection of barcoded reads in high throughput DNA sequencing data by controlling the false discovery rate.” *BMC Bioinformatics*. 2014;15:264. PMID: 25099007. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2105-15-264.

FINAL DECISION: YES
